newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Settlement signals end to U.S. arms ban on SAfrica.
newsitem.headline: Settlement signals end to U.S. arms ban on SAfrica.

text.p: The settlement of a court case against three South African firms accused of violating U.S. arms export laws signals the end of a 34-year-old weapons embargo imposed on the then apartheid state, South Africa said on Friday.

They said the resolution of the U.S. case brought in 1991 against state-owned Armscor, its subsidiary Kentron Party Ltd and a private firm, paved the way for greater military cooperation between the two countries.
"Relations will be normalised and the effect will be the end of the arms embargo," Ricky Naidoo, spokesman for South African deputy president Thabo Mbeki, told Reuters.

Armscor and Kentron on Thursday pleaded "no contest" in a U.S. District Court for Eastern Pennsylvania to breaking the arms embargo which since 1963 has banned American military equipment exports to South Africa.
The firms were charged with smuggling munitions, restricted commodities and technology made in the United States to South Africa between 1978 and 1989, using front companies.
Under U.S. law, a plea of no contest is treated as a guilty plea, although the defendant does not admit wrongdoing.

South Africa's Deputy Foreign Minister Aziz Pahad told a news conference on Friday that Washington had agreed that all restrictions on U.S. arms companies keen to export to South Africa, and on trade in the other direction, would be lifted once the case was settled.
"We believe that the resolution of the Armscor case opens up tremendous potential for South African companies to once again start interacting with U.S. companies," Pahad said.

Relations between the two countries were soured for a while this year when Pretoria said it might sell tank-firing and guidance systems to Syria, regarded by the United States as a state sponsor of terrorism. South Africa says it will now consult Washington over the deal.

Pahad said South Africa had not pleaded guilty to the charges as the present black-led government, which came to power in democratic elections in 1994, was not guilty of violations by the previous white regime.

Naidoo said the court decision, which will see the firms paying a total of $12.5 million to the U.S. government, was a "political settlement" and details of the resumption of arms trade between the two nations still needed to be ironed out.
Armscor has been fined $1 million and Kentron $500,000 on criminal charges. In addition the private Fuchs Electronics Ltd pleaded guilty on 11 related charges and was fined $10 million.
Additional fines totalling $6.25 million in lieu of civil penalties would also be paid by the firms to the South African government to establish an effective arms export control body.
